hints: Start by reminding yourself what each word means in plain language - what distance does speed involve, what distance does one wavelength represent, and what time does one frequency count?
Think about the time for just one complete oscillation and the distance the wave has travelled in that time, then combine them using speed = distance / time.
walkthrough:
**Recall what speed, wavelength and frequency really mean**
You can think of a wave as a moving pattern. Speed is always distance travelled divided by time taken, so $$v = \frac{d}{t}$$. Wavelength $\lambda$ is the length of one complete pattern - the distance between two neighbouring crests, or the distance the wave moves during one oscillation. Frequency $f$ is how many oscillations happen each second.

**Link frequency to the time for one wave**
If $f$ oscillations happen in 1 s, then the time for one oscillation, the period $T$, is $$T = \frac{1}{f}$$. In that time $T$ the wave must have moved forward by exactly one wavelength $\lambda$.

**Put distance and time into speed**
Now use speed = distance / time for this special distance and time: $$v = \frac{\lambda}{T}$$. Since $1/T = f$, this becomes $$v = f\lambda$$. That is the wave equation - distance per wave times waves per second gives distance per second.

Final answer: Speed $v = d/t$, wavelength $\lambda$ = distance for one oscillation, frequency $f$ = oscillations per unit time $= 1/T$. In time $T = 1/f$ wave travels distance $\lambda$, so $v = \lambda/T = f\lambda$.

hints: On a CRO the horizontal axis is time. Count how many horizontal divisions make up one complete sine wave from peak to next peak.
Convert that number of divisions into seconds using the 1.0 ms per division setting, then remember how period and frequency are linked.
walkthrough:
**Read the period from the trace**
Pick two matching points, for example one peak to the next peak. On Fig. 5.1 one full cycle spans 4 large divisions. Each division is $1.0\text{ ms}$, so $$T = 4.0 \times 1.0\text{ ms} = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}$$. It helps to measure over more than one cycle if you can to reduce reading error, but here one cycle is clear.

**Convert period to observed frequency**
Frequency is oscillations per second: $$f_o = \frac{1}{T}$$. So $$f_o = \frac{1}{4.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ s}} = 250\text{ Hz}$$. Notice this is higher than the source $236\text{ Hz}$ because the source is moving towards you - a classic Doppler shift.

hints: You now know the source frequency and the higher frequency heard by the stationary observer when the source approaches. Which Doppler formula connects these two frequencies to the source speed and wave speed?
Substitute $f_s = 236\text{ Hz}$, $f_o = 250\text{ Hz}$ and $v_s = 20\text{ m s}^{-1}$ into that relation and rearrange algebraically to isolate the wave speed $v$ before calculating.
walkthrough:
**Picture why the frequency is raised**
The source chases its own waves, so the waves ahead of it are squashed together. Wavelength in front is shortened, so a stationary observer meets more waves per second. For a source speed $v_s$ moving towards the observer: $$f_o = f_s \frac{v}{v - v_s}$$ where $v$ is the speed of sound.

**Solve for the speed of sound**
Insert the numbers you know: $f_s = 236\text{ Hz}$, $f_o = 250\text{ Hz}$, $v_s = 20\text{ m s}^{-1}$: $$250 = 236 \times \frac{v}{v - 20}$$. Rearrange: $$250(v-20) = 236v$$ $$250v - 5000 = 236v$$ $$14v = 5000$$. So $$v = \frac{5000}{14} \approx 360\text{ m s}^{-1}$$. This is a sensible order of magnitude for sound in air.
Final answer: For source approaching: $f_o = f_s v/(v - v_s)$. $250 = 236v/(v-20)$ giving $v = 360\text{ m s}^{-1}$ (2 s.f.).
